NeuroVision: An Automated Brain MRI Tumor Segmentation and
Quantitative Spatial Analysis System
Aditya Hatua,Amit Paul,Kritika Chakraborty,Diya Das,Dimitri Dey,Abhishek Kumar Gupta
ABSTRACT
The problem of segmenting brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images is a
difficult one in the field of medical image analysis because of the considerable morphological
heterogeneity found in terms of tumour size, geometric shape, anatomical location, and signal
intensity among different patients. Manually defining the areas of tumour takes a long time and
can lead to variations between different observers. In this paper a fully automated deep learning
approach for the segmentation of brain tumours and for their quantitative analysis using MRI data
is presented. The system makes use of a two-dimensional (2D) U-Net structure for segmenting the
tumour at the pixel level and is capable of handling both two-dimensional (2D) MRI scans and
three-dimensional (3D) volumetric neuroimaging data in NIfTI format. Once the segmentation has
been carried out, various image processing techniques are used to detect the tumour regions and
to extract quantitative features such as tumour area, centroid, bounding-box dimensions, radius,
and volume. When more than one tumour region is present, the spatial relationships between
them are assessed by means of centroid-to-centroid and boundary-to-boundary distance
measurements. The framework includes 2D visualisation, three-dimensional volumetric analysis,
and the automatic production of structured PDF and DOCX reports, thus offering an integrated
process from MRI input through to the quantitative results and visualisation. The system is
implemented as a web-based application that combines deep learning, computer vision,
volumetric analysis, and automated reporting. The proposed framework shows the potential of
bringing together segmentation and quantitative analysis in a single platform for a systematic
evaluation of brain MRI. The system is being developed as a research and decision-support
prototype and is not meant to replace professional clinical diagnosis.
Keywords: Brain tumor segmentation, magnetic resonance imaging, deep learning, U-Net,
medical image analysis, 2D MRI, 3D volumetric analysis, image processing, tumor morphometry,
spatial analysis
1. Introduction
Brain tumours are abnormal cell growths in the brain and present major difficulties in medical
diagnosis, in planning treatment and in monitoring the disease. It is essential to accurately
identify, localise and measure the areas of tumour in order to aid clinical assessment. Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI) is commonly used when examining the brain since it offers detailed
information about soft tissues. Yet automated analysis of MRI scans remains a challenge because
of the variations in tumour size, shape, position, intensity and appearance from patient to patient.
The evaluation of tumors generally depends heavily on manual examination and segmentation
carried out by qualified medical experts. While this method is effective, manual segmentation is
time-consuming and can lead to variations between observers. Apart from the tumor boundaries,
quantitative features such as area, volume, centroid, dimensions, and the spatial relationships
between several lesions are also valuable. Because of these limitations, there has been a push to
develop automated computer-aided techniques for medical image analysis.

Deep learning, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), has greatly advanced the field
of medical image segmentation, and U-Net is commonly employed in the segmentation of
biomedical images due to its encoder-decoder structure. The encoder is responsible for detecting
high-level features whilst the decoder gradually restores the spatial resolution in order to achieve
pixel-level segmentation. By means of its skip connections, detailed spatial information is passed
from the encoder to the decoder, which helps to maintain the boundaries of the tumour and the
finer features. Because of this, U-Net is well adapted for the segmentation of irregular structures
like brain tumours.
A two-dimensional U-Net model-based automated framework for the analysis of brain MRI
tumors is presented in this study. The U-Net model carries out pixel-level segmentation in order
to separate the tumor areas from the surrounding brain tissue; the segmentation masks thus
obtained are then processed to detect the individual tumor regions and to extract various
quantitative features such as area, centroid, bounding-box dimensions, radius, and volume.
The system is capable of handling both standard 2D MRI images and 3D NIfTI neuroimaging
volumes. When several tumor areas have been detected, the spatial relationships between them
are determined by calculating centroid-to-centroid and boundary-to-boundary distances.
Additionally, the system produces annotated visual representations of the segmentation results
and carries out volumetric analysis on the 3D MRI data.
A unified web-based workflow has been developed which allows MRI uploads, segmentation using
a U-Net method, quantitative analysis, visualization, study management, and the automatic
generation of PDF and DOCX reports. The framework brings together deep learning, image
processing and backend services in order to establish a structured method for the analysis of brain
MRI tumors.
The major contributions of this work are:
● A segmentation method based on U-Net: The use of a two-dimensional U-Net architecture
for segmentation at the pixel level of brain tumors.
● Support for 2D and 3D MRI: the processing of conventional MRI images and NIfTI
volumetric datasets.
● The quantitative analysis of tumours involves automatically extracting the area, the
centroid, the dimensions, the radius, and the volume.
● Analysis of the spatial relationship in the case of multiple tumours: calculation of the
distances between centroids and between boundaries.
● Visualization and reporting involve producing annotated segmentation results and
generating PDF/DOCX reports.
● A unified web-based system that integrates segmentation, image processing, analysis,
visualization, and reporting into one workflow.
The framework that has been proposed is to be used as a research and decision-support
prototype.

2. Background and Literature Survey
2.1 Background
A. Brain Tumor Analysis Using MRI
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) plays an important role in examining and analyzing brain
abnormalities due to its ability to produce detailed images of soft tissues and internal brain
structures. In brain tumor analysis, the main objective is to identify the tumor, determine its
boundaries, and evaluate its characteristics, including its location, size, and volume. Different MRI
sequences provide complementary information about the tumor and its surrounding tissues.
Among these, T1-weighted, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (T1ce), T2-weighted, and Fluid-
Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) images are widely used in brain tumor segmentation
research [1].
Manually identifying and outlining brain tumors in MRI scans can be challenging and time-
consuming, especially when tumors have irregular shapes, unclear boundaries, or multiple lesions
are present. These challenges have encouraged researchers to develop automated and semi-
automated methods that can make tumor segmentation more efficient and consistent. Among
the various approaches explored in medical image analysis, deep learning techniques have gained
significant attention. In particular, U-Net-based architectures have become widely used for brain
tumor segmentation because of their ability to learn complex image features and identify tumor
regions effectively. A systematic review of MRI-based brain tumor segmentation methods also
highlighted the growing importance of U-Net-based approaches in this field [1].
B. Medical Image Segmentation
Image segmentation is a technique used to divide an image into meaningful regions by assigning a
specific class or label to each pixel or voxel. In brain tumor analysis, the main purpose of
segmentation is to separate tumor regions from healthy brain tissue and other surrounding
structures. Accurate segmentation is essential for further analysis, as important measurements
such as tumor area, volume, centroid, and boundary characteristics depend on how precisely the
tumor region is identified.
Several traditional techniques have been used for image segmentation, including thresholding,
region growing, clustering, and edge-based methods. Although these techniques can be effective
in certain situations, they often struggle to identify brain tumors accurately because of variations
in image intensity, irregular tumor boundaries, differences in tissue appearance, and the complex
structure of tumor regions. With advances in deep learning, more effective segmentation
methods have been developed. These methods can automatically learn relevant features and
patterns from annotated medical images, helping them identify tumor regions more accurately
than some conventional approaches.

Page | 3
C. Deep Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely used in medical image analysis because they
can automatically learn important features and patterns from images at different levels. In brain
tumor segmentation, CNN-based methods help identify tumor regions by learning from annotated
MRI scans and generating segmentation maps at the pixel or voxel level. These models can
capture complex patterns in medical images, making them useful for distinguishing tumor tissue
from surrounding brain structures. Several studies have reviewed deep learning-based brain
tumor segmentation methods, discussing different network architectures, techniques for
addressing class imbalance, approaches for processing multiple MRI sequences, and other
strategies used to improve segmentation performance [2].
The Multimodal Brain Tumor Image Segmentation Benchmark (BraTS) has become an important
resource for developing and evaluating automated brain tumor segmentation methods. It
provides standardized MRI datasets along with expert-annotated tumor regions, enabling
researchers to compare the performance of different methods under consistent evaluation
settings [3]. To assess segmentation accuracy, researchers commonly use metrics such as the Dice
similarity coefficient, Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, and specificity. These measures provide
complementary information about how closely the predicted tumor regions match the reference
annotations and how effectively the model identifies tumor tissue.
D. U-Net Architecture
U-Net is a convolutional encoder-decoder network introduced by Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox
for biomedical image segmentation [4]. Its architecture consists of two main parts: a contracting
path (encoder) and an expanding path (decoder). The encoder captures important features from
the input image through successive convolution and downsampling operations, while the decoder
gradually recovers the spatial resolution to generate the final segmentation map.
One of the main features of U-Net is its use of skip connections, which link corresponding layers of
the encoder and decoder. These connections transfer spatial details from the encoder to the
decoder, helping the network retain important information about object boundaries and fine
image structures during segmentation. The original U-Net also showed that accurate biomedical
image segmentation could be achieved with a relatively small amount of annotated training data,
particularly when suitable data augmentation techniques were applied [4].
Due to its straightforward architecture and effectiveness in identifying image regions at the pixel
level, U-Net has become a widely adopted model for brain tumor segmentation. Over time,
researchers have proposed several variations to improve its performance and address the
limitations of the original architecture. These developments include residual connections,
attention mechanisms, dense connections, and transformer-based components, which aim to
improve feature extraction and capture more complex patterns in medical images [5].
E. Quantitative and Volumetric Tumor Analysis
Segmentation provides a binary or multi-class representation of the tumor region, but further
analysis is required to convert this representation into quantitative information. Morphological
analysis can be used to determine characteristics such as the area of a lesion, its bounding box,

centroid, radius, and other geometric properties. When volumetric MRI data are available, the
segmented regions can additionally be analyzed across multiple slices to obtain three-dimensional
measurements.
Quantitative tumor analysis is useful because it transforms a visual segmentation result into
structured numerical information. In the proposed framework, the segmentation output is
therefore followed by morphological and spatial analysis to characterize detected tumor regions
and their relationships.
F. 2D and 3D MRI Analysis
Brain MRI data can be represented as individual two-dimensional image slices or as three-
dimensional volumetric datasets. Two-dimensional segmentation approaches process individual
slices and can provide computational advantages compared with processing an entire 3D volume.
However, volumetric analysis provides additional spatial information across consecutive slices and
enables three-dimensional representation and measurement of anatomical structures.
Recent literature demonstrates the continued development of both 2D and 3D U-Net-based
approaches for brain tumor segmentation. Reviews of U-Net-based methods report that
researchers continue to investigate the trade-off between segmentation performance,
computational requirements, generalization, and the use of multimodal or volumetric information
[5], [6]. The proposed system follows a hybrid workflow in which a 2D U-Net is used for tumor
segmentation while 3D volumetric MRI data can be processed and analyzed as part of the broader
analysis pipeline.
2.2 Literary Review
Several deep learning-based approaches have been proposed for automated brain tumor
segmentation from MRI scans. Ronneberger et al. introduced U-Net, an encoder-decoder
convolutional neural network designed for biomedical image segmentation, which demonstrated
the effectiveness of skip connections for preserving spatial information [1].Since its introduction,
U-Net and its variants have been widely used for brain tumor segmentation due to their ability to
identify tumor regions and capture important spatial details in MRI scans.
Menze et al. contributed to the development of the Brain Tumor Image Segmentation Benchmark
(BraTS), which provides standardized multimodal MRI datasets and evaluation protocols to
support the assessment and comparison of automated brain tumor segmentation methods [2].
Building on this work, researchers have investigated various techniques to improve segmentation
performance, including advanced U-Net architectures, convolutional neural networks, attention
mechanisms, and three-dimensional segmentation approaches. These methods aim to improve
the accuracy and reliability of tumor identification across different MRI scans [3], [4].
Despite these advances, several challenges remain in automated brain tumor segmentation. Much
of the existing research focuses primarily on improving segmentation accuracy and evaluating
model performance using established benchmarks. However, further investigation is needed to
explore additional aspects of segmentation, such as the practical interpretation of results, the
reliability of tumor measurements, and the usefulness of the segmented regions for subsequent
analysis.

-- 5 of 29 --

Page | 5
Less emphasis is placed on integrating segmentation with detailed tumor morphometric
measurements, spatial relationships between multiple lesions, visualization, and automated
reporting within a single system.
The proposed work addresses this gap by combining 2D U-Net-based tumor segmentation with
quantitative morphological analysis, spatial analysis, 2D visualization, 3D volumetric analysis, and
automated report generation. This provides an integrated workflow that extends beyond
segmentation to produce structured and interpretable information from brain MRI data.
3. Methodology
The proposed system provides an integrated pipeline for automated brain tumor segmentation
and quantitative analysis from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. The overall methodology
consists of MRI data acquisition and preprocessing, deep learning-based tumor segmentation,
tumor region extraction, morphological analysis, spatial analysis, visualization, and automated
report generation. The system supports both two-dimensional (2D) MRI images and three-
dimensional (3D) volumetric neuroimaging data.
A. MRI Data Input and Preprocessing
The system accepts MRI data in commonly used image formats, including PNG and JPEG images,
as well as NIfTI files used for volumetric neuroimaging data. For 2D input, individual MRI images
are processed directly. For NIfTI volumes, the volumetric data are loaded and individual slices can
be extracted for subsequent processing.
Before segmentation, the input images undergo preprocessing to obtain a suitable representation
for the deep learning model. Image dimensions and intensity characteristics are standardized
according to the requirements of the segmentation pipeline. The preprocessed image is then
provided as input to the trained U-Net model.
B. U-Net-Based Tumor Segmentation
A two-dimensional U-Net architecture is employed for automatic tumor segmentation. U-Net
consists of an encoder path and a decoder path connected through skip connections. The encoder
extracts hierarchical features from the MRI image, while the decoder reconstructs the spatial
representation required to generate a pixel-level segmentation map.
When an MRI image is given as input to the trained U-Net model, the model predicts the regions
that are likely to contain a brain tumor. This process can be represented mathematically as
follows:
S=fθ(I)
where I represents the input MRI image, fθ denotes the trained U-Net model with its learned
parameters θ, and S represents the predicted tumor segmentation map.
The predicted segmentation map is then converted into a binary mask, in which tumor regions are
assigned a value of 1 and the background is assigned a value of 0. This binary mask clearly
separates the predicted tumor region from the surrounding background and is used for further
analysis, such as calculating the tumor area, estimating its size, and examining its shape and
boundaries.

-- 6 of 29 --

Page | 6
C. Tumor Region Extraction
After segmentation, the binary tumor mask is processed to identify separate tumor regions.
Image-processing techniques are then used to detect the boundaries of these regions and extract
their basic geometric properties.
For each detected tumor region, the system identifies its location and size and creates a
representation of the region for further analysis. This information can be used to study the
tumor's shape, boundaries, and spatial characteristics.
D. Morphological Analysis
After segmentation, the detected tumor regions are analyzed to measure their morphological
characteristics. These measurements provide useful information about the size, shape, and
location of each identified tumor region.
The system calculates the following parameters:
● Tumor area
● Bounding-box dimensions
● Centroid coordinates
● Radius
● Tumor volume
The centroid of a segmented tumor region represents its center and can be expressed as:
C=(Xc,Yc)
where Xc and Yc denote the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the center of the detected
tumor region, respectively.
When volumetric MRI data is available, the segmented tumor regions from multiple slices can be
combined to estimate the overall tumor volume. This approach provides a more complete
understanding of the tumor by considering its size and shape across different slices rather than
examining each two-dimensional (2D) image separately. As a result, the system can provide a
better representation of the tumor's overall size, spatial extent, and morphological characteristics.
E. Spatial Analysis of Multiple Tumors
When more than one tumor region is detected in an MRI image, the proposed system examines
the spatial relationship between the regions. The distance between the centers (centroids) of two
tumor regions is calculated using the Euclidean distance formula:
D_c = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
where C₁ = (x₁, y₁) and C₂ = (x₂, y₂) represent the centroids of the two detected tumor regions,
respectively.
Along with the centroid distance, the system also calculates the minimum distance between the
boundaries of the two regions. These measurements help determine how far apart the detected

-- 7 of 29 --

Page | 7
tumor regions are and provide a better understanding of their relative positions within the MRI
image.
F. 2D Visualization and 3D Volumetric Analysis
The segmentation results are displayed by overlaying the detected tumor regions on the original
MRI images. This helps users compare the original images with the model's predictions and
visually check whether the tumor regions have been identified correctly.
The system can also analyze three-dimensional (3D) MRI data by combining information from
multiple image slices. These results can be used to create a 3D representation of the tumor and
estimate its overall volume. Although the segmentation model processes each MRI slice
separately in 2D, combining the results from multiple slices provides a more complete view of the
tumor's size, shape, and spatial extent.
G. Automated Report Generation
After completing the segmentation and quantitative analysis, the obtained results are organized
into a structured report. The system generates reports in PDF and DOCX formats, which include
important analysis results, tumor measurements, and visual representations of the segmented
regions.
The reporting module presents the results in a clear and easy-to-understand format. This allows
users to review, save, and share the analysis results without needing to access the internal
processing steps of the system.
H. Integrated System Workflow
The proposed system processes MRI images through preprocessing and 2D U-Net segmentation to
identify tumor regions. The segmented regions are then analyzed to measure their size, shape,
and location. Finally, the results are visualized and compiled into an automated report in PDF or
DOCX format.
Workflow: MRI Input → Preprocessing → 2D U-Net Segmentation → Tumor Region Analysis →
Visualization → Report Generation.

The major data collection and preprocessing steps are as follows:
1. Dataset Composition:
The audited dataset contains 20 valid MRI–mask pairs, including 20 MRI images, 20
corresponding segmentation masks, and 20 unique patient identifiers. No errors were
reported during the dataset audit.
2. Dataset Verification:
Each MRI image is verified against its corresponding mask. The verification process checks
for missing files, unreadable images, dimensional mismatches, and invalid mask values.
3. Mask Processing:
The segmentation masks are converted into binary masks using the condition
mask>0mask > 0. This operation separates tumor regions from the background while
preserving the original source mask files.
4. Image Conversion:
Input MRI images are converted into grayscale format to provide a consistent single-
channel representation for the U-Net model.
5. Image Resizing:
All MRI images and their corresponding masks are resized to 256 × 256 pixels to maintain a
consistent image size during model training and prediction.
6. Intensity Normalization:
Each MRI image is normalized using its mean and standard deviation to reduce differences
in image intensity and provide more consistent input for the segmentation model.
7. Data Augmentation:
Data augmentation is applied only to the training images to increase their variety and help
prevent overfitting. The applied transformations include random rotation, changes in
image scale, and occasional adjustments to image intensity. Horizontal and vertical flipping
are not used in this experiment.
8. Image–Mask Alignment:
Whenever an MRI image is transformed, the same changes are applied to its

corresponding mask to ensure that the tumor regions remain correctly aligned with the
image.
9. Dataset Splitting:
The dataset is divided into three subsets: training, validation, and testing. A fixed random
seed of 42 is used to ensure that the split remains consistent and reproducible. The
dataset contains 14 training images, 3 validation images, and 3 test images.
10. Training and Evaluation:
The training set is used to train the U-Net model, while the validation set helps monitor its
performance during training. The test set is kept separate and used at the end to evaluate
how well the model performs on MRI images it has not seen before.
Preprocessing Pipeline
The preprocessing process starts by checking the MRI images and their masks. The images are
then converted to grayscale, resized to 256 × 256 pixels, and normalized. Data augmentation is
applied only to the training images to increase their variety. Finally, the dataset is divided into
training, validation, and testing sets.

Data Augmentation → Dataset Splitting
This process prepares the images and masks for training and evaluating the 2D U-Net model.
3.3 Architecture of Proposed Model
The proposed system uses a 2D U-Net model to identify tumor regions in MRI images. The model contains
convolution layers, batch normalization, and ReLU activation to extract image features. It also uses max pooling
to reduce image size, skip connections to preserve important details, and decoder layers to generate the final
segmentation. During prediction, the input image is resized to the required dimensions, and the model produces
a binary tumor mask using a sigmoid function and a threshold of 0.5. The resulting mask is then resized to match
the original image dimensions.
● Backend: The system uses FastAPI to handle image uploads, analysis, report generation, and health
checks. Uvicorn runs the application.
● Tumor segmentation: The system uses a trained U-Net model when a valid model file is available. If the
model path is missing or invalid, it uses a mock segmentation model (MockSegmentationModel v0.1)
instead.
● Image analysis: OpenCV, scikit-image, and SciPy are used to analyze the segmented regions. The
system identifies separate tumor regions and calculates their bounding boxes, centers, areas,
equivalent radii, maximum diameters, and distances between regions.
● Reports: ReportLab produces PDF reports and python-docx produces DOCX reports.
● Frontend: static HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla ES6 JavaScript served by the FastAPI application.

4.2 Limitations
1. Limited dataset size and diversity
The biggest limitation is the amount and diversity of MRI data used for training and evaluation.
If the model is trained on a relatively limited dataset, it may not generalize well to:
● different hospitals
● different MRI scanners
● different imaging protocols
● different patient populations
● different tumor appearances
A model can perform very well on its held-out dataset but perform differently on completely unseen external
data.
2. No external baseline comparison
Our project reports:
Metric NeuroVision U-Net
Dice 0.9600
IoU 0.9235
The current model achieved the reported Dice and IoU scores on the evaluated data.
3. Segmentation is not the same as diagnosis
The system primarily performs MRI-based brain tumor segmentation and identifies the suspected tumor
region. However, segmentation alone does not establish a definitive clinical diagnosis, tumor type, or
grade. Therefore, the system should be considered a decision-support tool and not a replacement for
radiologists or pathological diagnosis.
4. Limited MRI Sequence Information
Brain tumors can be evaluated using different MRI sequences, such as:
● T1
● T1-contrast
● T2
● FLAIR
● DWI/ADC
● SWI
● Perfusion

Our proposed system mainly uses a limited set of MRI sequence information. Therefore, it may not capture
all the clinically relevant characteristics of a tumor. This can affect the performance of our model, especially
in complex tumor cases.
5. Multiple tumors can be challenging
Our project aims to handle cases where more than one tumor may be present in the brain. However,
detecting multiple tumor regions can be challenging.
MRI→T1,T2,T3,…,Tn
The system needs to correctly distinguish the following parameters:
● separate tumors
● connected tumor regions
● edema
● necrotic areas
● normal anatomical structures
Small or closely positioned lesions can be particularly difficult to separate correctly.
6. Small tumors are harder to detect.
Large tumors cover more pixels in an MRI image, making them easier for the model to detect and segment.
In contrast, small tumors may be harder to identify because they occupy fewer pixels.
For a small tumor:
Tumor Area≪Brain Area
Even a small boundary error can significantly affect Dice and IoU.
For example, if a tumor contains only a few hundred pixels, incorrectly predicting several dozen pixels can
noticeably reduce the segmentation score.
7. Image preprocessing impacts performance
Our pipeline prepares and preprocesses the MRI images before performing segmentation.
Differences in:
● image resolution
● intensity range
● contrast
● orientation
● normalization
● image size
● MRI acquisition protocol
can affect the model's prediction.

This work presented an integrated deep learning-based framework for automated brain tumor segmentation
and quantitative analysis from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed approach combines a two-
dimensional U-Net segmentation model with image processing, morphological analysis, spatial analysis,
volumetric analysis, visualization, and automated reporting to provide a complete MRI analysis workflow. Unlike
approaches that focus exclusively on generating a segmentation mask, the proposed framework extends the
analysis by extracting measurable tumor characteristics such as area, centroid, dimensions, radius, and volume,
while also determining spatial relationships between multiple detected lesions.
The framework supports both conventional two-dimensional MRI images and three-dimensional NIfTI-based
volumetric data. Segmentation results can be visualized over the original MRI data, while quantitative outputs
are organized into structured reports in PDF and DOCX formats.
This project combines deep learning-based segmentation with traditional image-processing and visualization
techniques to convert MRI images into useful analytical results. It provides a single platform for identifying
tumor regions, analyzing their features, and presenting the results in a structured format.
The proposed system serves as a research prototype for computer-aided brain MRI analysis. However, it is not
intended to replace professional medical diagnosis. Its performance depends on the quality and variety of the
data used for training and testing.
In the future, the system can be improved by using larger and more diverse datasets, including multiple MRI
sequences, and developing better 3D tumor visualization. Its performance can also be evaluated using standard
segmentation metrics and independent datasets. Further improvements, such as support for standard medical
imaging formats and integration with clinical systems, along with proper clinical validation, could make the
system more useful in practical settings.
Overall, this project provides a foundation for developing more reliable and user-friendly tools for brain tumor
segmentation and MRI analysis.
